title: The millionth domino
hook: Nobody can push a million dominoes by hand. So how could we know the millionth falls?

knows: what it means for a statement to be true for one number
doesNotKnow: what proof by induction is: a start plus a step rule covers every whole number

misconception: Proving something for every whole number needs checking each number, so it can never be finished.
objective: The learner can say that a start (true for 1) and a step (true for n means true for n + 1) together make a statement true for every whole number, and that a single broken step stops the chain.

claims.text: With every link intact, pushing domino 1 knocks down all 12; with domino 6 out of reach, dominoes 1 to 5 fall and 6 to 12 stand.
claims.source: Demo.tsx fallen(pushed, broken): N = 12 when the chain is intact, GAP_AT − 1 = 5 when domino 6 is moved 44 px further than a domino's 52 px reach. A model, not physics.

claims.text: If domino 1 falls, and whenever one falls the next does, then every domino falls: 2 falls, so 3 falls, and so on past any number you name.
claims.source: Principle of mathematical induction (an axiom of the natural numbers in Peano arithmetic; equivalent to the well-ordering principle).

claims.text: Proof by induction: prove a statement for 1, prove that true for n means true for n + 1, and it holds for every whole number.
claims.source: Standard statement of induction, e.g. any discrete mathematics text (Rosen, Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications, 5.1).

claims.text: The dominoes picture induction; they do not prove it.
claims.source: Brief 43 claim (2): the domino image is an analogy. A finite row cannot show infinitely many cases.

recall.question: A rule is true for 1, and whenever it is true for some number it is also true for the next. What do you still need to check?
options: Nothing: it holds for every whole number
Each number up to a million
recall.why: The start and the step make a chain: 1, then 2, then 3, and on forever. That is proof by induction.
